---
title: "Native C++ biological neural-network foundation"
---

This page documents the current native C++ modeling surface in the optional
`Cellerator::nn` component. It complements the
[Python-facing NN foundation guide](nn_foundation.qmd); the C++ API is designed
for native model authoring rather than generated from Python classes. Both sit
within Cellerator's [biological machine-learning scope](scope.qmd) and
[modeling architecture](architecture.qmd#cpp-and-python-modeling).

The native Cell contract is a separate, Torch-free interface at
[`<Cellerator/cell.hh>`](../include/Cellerator/cell.hh). A Cell is a continuing
virtual instance: it binds a shared model to instance-specific information,
independently of its physical layout or device placement. Its representation
can be a borrowed row, pooled state, a structured owner, or a handle to
separately placed portions. Python's existing Cell API is unchanged.

The optional NN component uses C++20 and ATen/LibTorch tensors. Python is
optional; LibTorch supplies tensor operations, ordinary optimizers, and
autograd. Native models remain ordinary C++ callables with their own result
types. The Cell core itself uses C++17 and the standard library only.

The separate experimental [factorized joint-interaction component](factorized_interactions.qmd)
provides native CUDA preparation and an explicit conditional joint forward/VJP
without a Torch dependency. Its numerical law, lifetimes and source-bound
qualification are distinct from the conventional NN components on this page.

## Bind a continuing native instance

`Cell<Model, Instance, ModelHandle = Model*>` stores the selected model handle
and instance value. It adds no mandatory virtual base, allocation, identity,
clock, trajectory, device, cache, or mutation tracker. Model and instance types
are independent, so the same model can support different representations.

```cpp
#include <Cellerator/cell.hh>

struct Reading { double value; };
struct Scale {
    double weight;
    double operator()(Reading& instance, double input) const {
        instance.value += input;
        return weight * instance.value;
    }
};

Scale model{2.0};
auto cell = cellerator::make_cell(model, Reading{1.0});
auto prediction = cell.forward(3.0); // 8.0; the same instance now contains 4.0
```

`make_cell(model, instance)` borrows an lvalue model and stores a decayed
instance value, copying an lvalue or moving an rvalue. The model must outlive
the Cell. Passing an explicit `std::shared_ptr<Model>` instead retains shared
model ownership; null owners are rejected. Copying a Cell follows its stored
instance and handle semantics: a row or pooled handle can alias storage, while
an owning representation can duplicate private information or forbid copying.
No operation implicitly clones state or generates a biological identity.

`forward(args...)` invokes `model(instance, args...)` and preserves the exact
result, including references, `void`, move-only values, and completion handles.
Const forwarding requires a callable accepting a const model and const
instance. `model()` and `instance()` expose const-correct lvalue references.
Temporary access is rejected; moved-from Cells require reassignment before
further operations unless their model and instance explicitly permit more.

Logical in-place mutation does not require overwriting the same physical
buffers. A model can replace a state tensor while retaining earlier values for
backward, share a prefix, or relocate a portion through its owner. Models and
owners define cache validity, parameter revisions, asynchronous readiness,
retained-result lifetimes, and exception guarantees. Cell adds no automatic
rollback or synchronization. A reference returned by an operation is valid
only under that operation's lifetime contract.

### Typed information access

A representation can expose ordinary public hooks
`View read(ViewTag<View>) const &` and
`View write(ViewTag<View>) &`. `cell.view<View>()` and `cell.edit<View>()`
delegate to those hooks. `supports<View>()` and `supports_edit<View>()` detect
contracts at compile time; an unsupported typed acquisition is ill-formed.
Reads require lvalues and edits require mutable lvalues. Capability presence
does not establish data readiness, bounds validity, or cache freshness.

The event and expression headers provide `EventPrefix`, `DenseExpressionRow`,
and `MutableDenseExpressionRow`. These are storage selections, not complete
Cells: bind a model to one, or include it in a richer instance representation.
They borrow stable buffer or matrix descriptor objects, retain typed
application identities, and reacquire pointers when producing views. Event
prefixes preserve order and repeated occurrences. Dense rows preserve scalar
type, feature IDs, explicit stride, and padding. Numeric writes use an explicit
edit view; feature identity and layout remain read-only through that view.
The expression adapter uses C++20 `std::span`.

Descriptors retain native placement metadata and cause no transfer or host
dereference of device data. The owner controls allocation, synchronization,
reordering, and invalidation of existing borrowed views. Physical offsets are
storage locations, not universal biological IDs. Caller-defined views need no
central registry, and representations without views need no access boilerplate.

### Optional runtime access

Include [`<Cellerator/cells/access.hh>`](../include/Cellerator/cells/access.hh)
when a heterogeneous consumer needs runtime view discovery. `CellViews` is the
polymorphic access boundary, with protected `CellAccess<View>` and
`CellEdit<View>` implementation hooks. An explicit borrowed bridge exposes only
the selected capabilities:

```cpp
// event_cell is a typed Cell whose instance supplies EventView.
auto bridge = cellerator::make_cell_views<
    cellerator::CellAccess<EventView>>(event_cell);
const cellerator::CellViews& runtime = bridge;
auto events = runtime.view<EventView>();
```

Selected bridge contracts must be supported by the source; a const source
cannot supply edits. Other runtime requests throw `std::bad_cast`, and runtime
capability checks return false. The bridge borrows the Cell object: that object
must outlive it and remain at the same address. Returned views separately obey
their backing-storage contracts. The bridge cannot bind a temporary Cell.

The typed path uses no RTTI or virtual call and needs no runtime destructor
link. The optional runtime path performs one RTTI lookup and virtual dispatch
per view acquisition and links `Cellerator::libCellerator` for `CellViews`'s
out-of-line destructor. These are structural costs, not measured speedups.

[`event_forward.cc`](../examples/native_cell/event_forward.cc) demonstrates
storage-owned append extending the same Cell's prefix and returning an
operation result. Copied prefix selections retain earlier boundaries; stale
and foreign continuations are rejected. Its evaluator is deterministic
scaffolding, not a scientific Karyoplast model.
[`multimodal.cc`](../examples/native_cell/multimodal.cc) combines event,
expression, identity, and custom views with an optional runtime bridge.
[`foundation.cc`](../examples/native_cell/foundation.cc) explores shared and
pooled portions, joint operations, host placement choices, cache revisions, and
resource-retaining asynchronous results. Its supplied cost estimates do not
constitute a placement engine or performance qualification. See the
[host build route](developer_reference.qmd#native-cell-examples).

## Author a model as an ordinary C++ type

A model can be a struct with an `operator()` and concrete components. There is
no required model superclass, `torch::nn::Module`, member walk, parameter
registration, or universal tensor-valued forward result. The reference
[`ExpressionReferenceModel`](../examples/native_nn/reference_models.hh)
contains explicit `Parameters`, groups, a feature encoder, attention, a linear
projection, and a target-bound readout. Its base call keeps the composition
visible:

```cpp
auto encoded = encoder(
    nn::FeatureInput{ids, values, observed, std::nullopt}, run);
auto features = encoded + interactions(encoded, nn::AttentionLayout{}, run);
auto expression = expression_projection(features, run).squeeze(-1);
auto pooled = nn::mean_by_group(
    features.reshape({features.size(0) * features.size(1), width}),
    repeated_group_offsets(features.size(0), features.size(1)));
return ExpressionResult{
    std::move(expression), std::move(features), std::move(pooled),
    feature_binding.canonical_ids(), batch.sample_ids};
```

Here `ExpressionResult` is a model-specific C++ record with expression values
`[samples, features]`, per-feature representations `[samples, features, width]`,
a caller-selected pooled view `[samples, width]`, and feature/sample identities.
Returning it does not require wrapping it in
`nn::Prediction`. That wrapper is available when a boundary needs typed query
labels. The complete expression and event-history compositions are in the
[reference models](../examples/native_nn/reference_models.hh), with their
small CPU training loops in [`train.cc`](../examples/native_nn/train.cc). The
event-history model builds packed `[START, e0, ..., e(n-2)]` inputs, keeps
repeated event occurrences distinct, applies a prepared causal relation, and
returns packed logits plus per-history features. Empty histories retain a START
representation but have no next-event target.

## Make parameter ownership explicit

[`parameters.hh`](../include/Cellerator/nn/parameters.hh) defines `nn::Parameters`
as the owner of parameter slots. Components allocate through cheap, copyable
`nn::ParameterGroup` handles; groups can be kept separate, frozen, or made
trainable explicitly. Slot IDs and structural layout are available for
inspection, and tied slots resolve to the same leaf tensor. Nothing discovers
parameters by walking arbitrary model fields.

The reference training code passes the owner's unique leaf tensors to an
ordinary Torch optimizer:

```cpp
torch::optim::Adam optimizer(
    model.parameters.torch_parameters(), torch::optim::AdamOptions(0.025));
for (std::int64_t step = 0; step < steps; ++step) {
    optimizer.zero_grad();
    const auto loss = expression_loss(model, batch, true);
    if (!loss) throw std::runtime_error("expression supervision disappeared");
    loss->backward();
    optimizer.step();
}
```

`nn::Run{true}` selects training behavior such as dropout. It does not enable
or disable autograd; gradient recording and optimizer steps remain controlled
by the normal Torch mechanisms. `ParameterGroup::set_trainable(false)` freezes
that group's leaves while leaving gradients through the computation to inputs
connected. `torch_parameters()` returns each distinct owner leaf once, in slot
order, including frozen leaves.

`ParameterGroup::parameter_ids()` exposes a borrowed span of that group's owner
slots; `group.torch_parameters()` selects its unique leaves for an optimizer.
Group checkpoint overloads save and restore just those leaves using local slot
IDs. Intentionally tied leaves remain shared with any other groups. Adding an
existing parameter adopts the same leaf handle and rejects implicit device or
dtype conversions; detach, cast, and placement choices are explicit.

Several functional forms accept borrowed tensors instead of allocating slots:
[`layers.hh`](../include/Cellerator/nn/layers.hh) exposes
`nn::LinearParameters`, which can refer to caller-owned weight and bias tensors;
[`features.hh`](../include/Cellerator/nn/features.hh) and
[`attention.hh`](../include/Cellerator/nn/attention.hh) provide corresponding
functional parameter records. These calls do not move, clone, or register the
borrowed tensors. The caller keeps their ownership and lifetime.
By contrast, `Parameters` owns its slots, `PreparedRelation` copies its host CSR
structure and owns its realized device buffers, and `PreparedTargets` owns its
prepared index tensors. Query payload feature IDs and observation coordinates
are borrowed views; keep their declarations alive while using a result built
from an lvalue request. An rvalue request is retained by the returned payload,
though any lvalue objects referenced by that request must still outlive it.

The queried `predict` path retains one typed lifetime frame per batched call.
It holds the base result, rvalue model/input/request values, selector-produced
values, and user-defined full-head results whose gathers may return borrowed
views. Multiple predictions share that frame; there is no per-prediction owner
allocation. An rvalue conditioned invocation needs one additional retained
owner because a conditioner can return a view into its input even by value.
Lvalue dependencies remain caller-owned. Direct model and decoder composition
avoids these retention allocations and leaves result lifetimes explicit; normal
numerical operations still have their ordinary allocation costs.

## Bind biological identities at the boundary

[`biology::FeatureBinding`](../include/Cellerator/biology/feature_binding.hh)
resolves canonical biological identities to model rows. Its preparation returns
[`execution::FeatureSourceBinding`](../include/Cellerator/execution/dependency/feature_binding.hh),
which records source gather positions, canonical indices when supplied, model
indices, and an optional projected physical map. These are coordinates for
aligning values; the caller retains the numerical storage.
`FeatureInput::ids` are numerical model rows; they are not canonical IDs. The
caller prepares the binding and aligns measurements before passing tensors to
the encoder. A source position, biological identity, model index, occurrence
ordinal, and physical offset are different coordinates.

The native C++ types keep logical structure separate from its physical
realization:

- [`structure::LogicalAxis`](../include/Cellerator/structure/identity.hh)
  declares a semantic domain, logical order, and extent. It does not declare a
  partition, geometry, or buffer.
- [`structure::OccurrenceCoordinates`](../include/Cellerator/structure/coordinates.hh)
  declares ordered identities, group offsets, an optional logical axis, and a
  structure generation. Repeated identities are valid occurrences.
  `structure::OccurrenceOrderToken` identifies that exact declaration, so
  equal extents do not make distinct orders compatible.
- [`layout::AxisBinding`](../include/Cellerator/layout/axis_binding.hh)
  associates physical geometry and partition identities with a logical axis.
  [`layout::OccurrenceMap`](../include/Cellerator/layout/occurrence_map.hh)
  associates occurrence ordinals with physical buffer positions and retains
  the order token it was built for.
- `execution::FeatureSourceBinding` is the prepared source-to-model mapping.
  `FeatureBinding::prepare(...)` aligns a unique feature axis;
  `FeatureBinding::map_occurrences(...)` maps occurrences independently and
  retains repeated identities. Neither path owns or coerces the value tensor.

`FeatureBindingOptions` and `FeatureBindingDescriptor` keep `axis` (the
`structure::LogicalAxis`) separate from `physical_axis` (the
`layout::AxisBinding`). Native descriptor serialization keeps no-axis and
full, nonempty physical-axis records at schema version 1. Version 2 represents
logical-only axes and zero-extent axes; a zero-extent physical binding retains
its geometry and partition identities. This descriptor capability does not relax
`FeatureBinding::from_ids`' requirement for at least one canonical identity.
The current Python `FeatureBinding.from_manifest` reader accepts version 1 and
explicitly rejects native version 2; the C++ namespace split does not add a
Python axis or layout API.

For example, an ordered source `("gene-B", "gene-A", "gene-B")` can map to
model indices `(11, 7, 11)` while an `OccurrenceMap` maps its occurrence
ordinals `(0, 1, 2)` to physical buffer positions `(2, 0, 1)`. Reordering the
buffer changes that physical map, not the logical identities or model mapping.

```cpp
#include <Cellerator/biology/feature_binding.hh>
#include <Cellerator/layout/occurrence_map.hh>
#include <Cellerator/structure/coordinates.hh>

#include <cassert>
#include <cstdint>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    using Identity = std::string;
    const cellerator::structure::LogicalAxis source_axis{
        cellerator::structure::domain_id{1, 0},
        cellerator::structure::order_id{2, 0}, 3};
    const auto source =
        cellerator::structure::OccurrenceCoordinates<Identity>::from_ids(
            std::vector<Identity>{"gene-B", "gene-A", "gene-B"},
            std::vector<std::int64_t>{0, 3}, source_axis);
    const cellerator::layout::AxisBinding physical_axis{
        source_axis, cellerator::structure::geometry_id{3, 0},
        cellerator::structure::partition_id{4, 0}};
    const auto physical = cellerator::layout::OccurrenceMap::from_positions(
        source.order_token(), std::vector<std::int64_t>{2, 0, 1}, physical_axis);
    const auto genes = cellerator::biology::FeatureBinding<Identity>::from_ids(
        std::vector<Identity>{"gene-A", "gene-B"},
        std::vector<std::int64_t>{7, 11});
    const auto prepared = genes.map_occurrences(source, &physical);
    assert((prepared.source_positions() == std::vector<std::int64_t>{0, 1, 2}));
    assert((prepared.model_indices() == std::vector<std::int64_t>{11, 7, 11}));
    assert((prepared.physical_positions() == std::vector<std::int64_t>{2, 0, 1}));
}
```

`nn::FeatureEncoder` combines model-row embeddings with optional values,
observation status, and aligned attributes. Its `FeatureInput` explicitly
contains `ids`, optional `values`, optional Boolean `observed`, and optional
`attributes`. It does not infer aliases, normalize measurements, rank features,
or assign biological meaning to integer rows.

For ordered or repeated participants, use `structure::OccurrenceCoordinates`
and pass any physical placement separately through `layout::OccurrenceMap`.

[`PreparedRelation`](../include/Cellerator/nn/relations.hh) binds CSR support
to source and target occurrence-order tokens, group declarations, structural
generation, and an explicit device.
CSR rows address target occurrence ordinals and columns address source
occurrence ordinals. Optional layout bindings preserve the physical
realization separately.
Preparation owns copies of host structure and can explicitly realize it on a
device with `.to(device)`; duplicate edges and empty neighborhoods are
retained. `.causal()` constructs a prefix-only relation while preserving its
declared endpoints. A change to endpoint order, topology, grouping, generation,
or device requires a compatible prepared relation; changes to feature values
alone do not redefine that structure.

## Compose interactions, readouts, and learning questions

[`attention.hh`](../include/Cellerator/nn/attention.hh) defines
`nn::RelationAttention`, which supports dense grouped layouts and prepared
relations. The default `AttentionKernel::aten` implementation is differentiable
ATen; `AttentionKernel::cellerator_csr` opts into the staged CSR CUDA kernel
described under [backend limits](#native-operations-and-limits).
`nn::InteractionPrograms` adds learned queries over features and can use a
caller-prepared overlapping relation.
[`programs.hh`](../include/Cellerator/nn/programs.hh) defines this composition
and `nn::GatedInteractor`, which supplies a separate composition for
independently gated participant occurrences. These components compute the
relationships the caller declares; they do not infer a hard regulatory
topology or establish causal interpretation.

Readouts are also concrete values. `nn::readout(decoder, selector, binding)`
combines a decoder with a selector for the model result and a target binding.
The selector can be a member pointer, as in the example below.
[`query.hh`](../include/Cellerator/nn/query.hh) provides the typed request
composer. A `query` request supplies prepared target identities and
`nn::ObservationCoordinates`; `nn::predict` invokes the base model once and
evaluates the requested readouts against that same result:

```cpp
auto view = nn::readout(model.atac_readout,
                        &ex::ExpressionResult::pooled,
                        model.atac_binding);
auto targets = model.atac_binding.prepare(
    model.atac_binding.canonical_ids());
auto request = nn::query(view, targets, coordinates);
auto prediction = nn::predict(model, batch, nn::Run{training}, request);
```

For repeated queries on a device, `nn::prepare_targets(binding, requested_ids,
device)` creates `PreparedTargets` with reusable model-index and output-column
tensors. A plain `binding.prepare(...)` is a host alignment; the direct
`FeatureReadout` overload materializes its index tensor during each call.
Calling a `Readout` directly returns the decoder's value type. The optional
`Prediction` wrapper is added at the query boundary by `nn::predict`.

[`readouts.hh`](../include/Cellerator/nn/readouts.hh) implements
`FeatureReadout`, a query-capable head that selects the requested target
embedding rows and computes those outputs. A conventional full-output head can
instead compute all outputs and gather requested columns afterward. The
returned `Prediction<Values, Payload>` keeps the head's value type and adds
optional feature and observation coordinates; ordinary model calls remain free
to return custom types.

`nn::conditioned(model, input, conditioner, condition)` makes numerical
conditioning an explicit call: the conditioner receives the input and
condition and produces the actual input passed to the model. Descriptive
observation coordinates only label predictions; they are not silently used as
conditioning. For tensor-valued predictions,
`align_prediction_targets` aligns target feature IDs and sample/window groups,
and `categorical_target_columns` maps event labels to prediction class columns.
[`supervision.hh`](../include/Cellerator/nn/supervision.hh) provides these
alignment helpers. `reduce_prediction_loss` requires a declared
`SupervisionUnit::observation` or `SupervisionUnit::cell`. Observation
reduction weights valid scalar loss terms equally; cell reduction pools valid
terms within each physical cell and then weights valid cells equally, requiring
physical cell IDs separately from sample/window IDs. These helpers align or
reduce a caller-defined objective rather than choosing one for every model.

The [training example](../examples/native_nn/train.cc) shows ordinary optimizer
loops for masked expression prediction, next-event prediction, and auxiliary
ATAC readouts with either a frozen or jointly trained base. Its fixtures are
synthetic examples of API composition, not biological validation or a
prescribed model architecture.

## Native operations and limits

The focused numerical adapters declared in
[`ops.hh`](../include/Cellerator/nn/ops.hh) retain narrow contracts:

- `product2_cpu` is CPU FP32 over a one-dimensional input, coefficients, and
  int64 index arrays; it supplies first-order gradients only.
- `grouped_linear_cuda` takes CUDA FP16 or FP32 input and expert weights plus
  host row offsets; empty expert segments are supported and autograd is
  first-order only.
- Staged CSR scaled-dot-product attention is an explicit CUDA path with matching
  FP16/FP32 payloads, FP32 accumulation, and first-order gradients. It currently
  requires zero dropout. The default attention kernel remains ATen.

These adapter contracts do not limit ordinary ATen compositions to the same
shapes or derivative behavior. Source availability and a successful host build
do not establish GPU qualification, performance improvement, or biological
validity. The [adapter record](../planning/native-nn-foundation-2026-10-31/derivatives/REPORT.md)
and [composition record](../planning/native-nn-foundation-2026-10-31/derivatives/COMPOSITION_REPORT.md)
contain bounded V100 correctness/memcheck results for captured executables.
Later host-only changes are recorded separately; this page makes no performance
or biological claim.

## Headers, CMake, and optional host modules

The canonical header entry point is
[`<Cellerator/nn.hh>`](../include/Cellerator/nn.hh), with focused declarations
under [`include/Cellerator/nn`](https://github.com/tumlinso/Cellerator/tree/main/include/Cellerator/nn).
Biological identity resolution remains under `biology`; logical identities and
occurrences live under `structure`, physical bindings under `layout`, and
prepared source mappings under `execution`. The optional
C++20 `Cellerator::nn` target is independent of Python bindings but depends on
LibTorch and the native Product2 target. A standalone CPU configure can enable
the component and reference executable:

```sh
cmake -S . -B /tmp/cellerator-native-nn \
  -DCELLERATOR_ENABLE_CUDA=OFF \
  -DCELLERATOR_ENABLE_NN=ON \
  -DCELLERATOR_ENABLE_NN_CUDA=OFF \
  -DCELLERATOR_ENABLE_PYTHON=OFF \
  -DCELLERATOR_ENABLE_TORCH=OFF \
  -DCELLERATOR_BUILD_PRODUCT2=ON \
  -DCELLERATOR_BUILD_NN_TRAIN=ON
cmake --build /tmp/cellerator-native-nn --target cellerator_nn native_nn_train
/tmp/cellerator-native-nn/native_nn_train
```

Configure with `Torch_DIR` or `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` for the local LibTorch
installation as needed. The
[standalone build and installed-consumer route](../planning/native-nn-foundation-2026-10-31/build/README.md)
records the environment-specific CMake invocation. Enabling the CUDA adapters
is separate and also requires Cellerator framework CUDA, a loaded CUDA
toolchain, and CUDA-enabled Torch.

An optional `CelleratorNNModules` package re-exports selected public declarations
through the C++20 module [`cellerator.nn`](../modules/native/cellerator.nn.ccm);
its separate [CMake project](../modules/native/CMakeLists.txt) is CXX-only.
The module is a host C++ import surface, not an NVCC module entry point. Use
the ordinary public headers in CUDA translation units. The optional module
packaging does not change the underlying C++ types or ABI.

For Python-facing behavior and its distinct implementation boundary, see the
[Python NN foundation guide](nn_foundation.qmd). The shared goals and remaining
modeling questions are recorded in the
[architecture](architecture.qmd#modeling-and-neural-network-backbone); the
code links above define the native interfaces described on this page.
